summary: In Greek mythology, Galene (Ancient Greek Γαλήνη, "calm weather" or "tranquility") is a minor sea goddess and Nereid who personifies calm seas. Hesiod names her among the fifty daughters of Nereus and Doris; Pausanias saw a statue of Galene beside Thalassa in the temple of Poseidon at Corinth. She is sometimes linked with, but kept distinct from, her sister Galatea.
etymology: Galene (Γαλήνη) means "calm weather," "calm," or "tranquility" — the stillness of a windless sea.

sections.heading: Nereid of calm seas
paragraphs: Hesiod (Theogony 244) enumerates Galene among the Nereids. Euripides mentions "Galaneia" as a daughter of Pontus, and Callimachus refers to "Galenaia," extending the calm-sea personification beyond the Hesiodic list. Pausanias (2.1.9) records a statue of Galene next to Thalassa among the offerings in Poseidon's temple at Corinth.
Modern scholarship sometimes notes a possible identity with Galatea; the atlas keeps Galene (galene) and the Sicilian Nereid Galatea (galatea-nymph) as separate nodes.

sections.heading: Other Galenes
paragraphs: A maenad named Galene appears on a vase painting — a cultic namesake, not this sea nymph. The main-belt asteroid 427 Galene takes its name from the mythological figure.

cultCenters: Corinth (statue in the temple of Poseidon, with Thalassa)
